cards.front: Which locator should you reach for first on an interactive element?
cards.back: `getByRole()` with a `name`. It finds the element the way a user perceives it, so it survives class renames and layout changes.

cards.front: What happens when an action runs on a locator that matches several elements?
cards.back: It throws a strict mode violation. Narrow the locator instead of adding `.first()`, which only hides the ambiguity.

cards.front: What does `click()` wait for before acting?
cards.back: The element must be attached, visible, stable, enabled, and able to receive events.

cards.front: Why must a web-first assertion be awaited?
cards.back: Without `await` it keeps retrying in the background while the test moves on, so it can't fail the test.

cards.front: What makes the `getBy*` locators a good first choice?
cards.back: They find elements by user-facing meaning: role, accessible name, label, placeholder, or visible text. Tests read better and survive CSS and DOM changes, and role and label locators rely on the same information as assistive technology.

cards.front: What does `getByRole()` match, and how do you narrow it?
cards.back: An ARIA role, including implicit roles from native HTML. Narrow it with the accessible name, as in `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save', exact: true })`. The name can come from visible text, a label, or an ARIA attribute.

cards.front: Which locator suits a form field that has a label?
cards.back: `getByLabel('Email address')`. It uses the description users see and doesn't depend on the field's position or styling.

cards.front: Do `getBy*` locators replace accessibility testing?
cards.back: No. A failing locator can reveal a missing name or role, but it is not an audit. You still need dedicated accessibility checks.

cards.front: When is a CSS selector the right choice?
cards.back: When no user-facing locator fits, or a short stable attribute is the clearest hook. Prefer something like `input[type="password"]` over long chains tied to layout.

cards.front: Why are deeply nested CSS selectors brittle?
cards.back: They encode the exact parent-child structure and position, so a harmless markup change breaks them even though the page still behaves the same for users.

cards.front: How do you use XPath in Playwright, and when might you?
cards.back: Pass it to `locator()`, as in `page.locator('//button[@type="submit"]')`. Selectors starting with `//` or `..` are detected as XPath, and an `xpath=` prefix makes it explicit. It can express ancestry, but complex expressions are hard to maintain.

cards.front: How does `getByText()` match by default, and how do you make it exact?
cards.back: By default it matches a case-insensitive substring and normalizes whitespace. Pass `{ exact: true }` for a whole, case-sensitive match, or a regular expression for text that varies.

cards.front: How do you narrow buttons to the one containing "Submit"?
cards.back: `page.getByRole('button').filter({ hasText: 'Submit' })`. If the button has a reliable accessible name, `getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` is simpler.

cards.front: What does `getByTestId()` look for, and how do you change it?
cards.back: `data-testid` by default. Set `testIdAttribute` in the Playwright config to use another attribute, such as `data-pw`. Test ids are stable hooks, but they shouldn't replace meaningful roles and labels.

cards.front: A link has no accessible name, only `class="shopping_cart_link"` and `data-test="shopping-cart-link"`. What do you do?
cards.back: Use `page.locator('.shopping_cart_link')`, or configure `testIdAttribute` to `data-test` and use `getByTestId()`. Also report the missing name: fixing it helps users and allows a role locator.

cards.front: A locator unexpectedly matches several elements. How do you make it reliable?
cards.back: Scope it to a meaningful container, then use a distinguishing property: `page.locator('form').getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })`. Use `.first()` or positions only when order is the behavior under test.

cards.front: How would you improve `#app > div:nth-child(2) > button` for a Save button?
cards.back: Use `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`, scoped to a named dialog or form if there are several. It describes the control as a user identifies it, not where it sits in the DOM.

cards.front: When should a text or role locator use a regular expression?
cards.back: When part of the text is stable and part legitimately varies, such as a greeting with a first name. Keep it specific enough to avoid unrelated matches, and use exact strings when the full value is stable.

cards.front: How do you choose between a role locator, a test id, and CSS?
cards.back: Start with role and name, or a label for form controls. Use a test id when there is no semantic hook. Use CSS for a simple, stable case that is awkward to express otherwise, and keep any fallback short.

cards.front: Two buttons are named "Continue", one in the main page and one in a dialog. How do you click the main page one?
cards.back: Scope the role locator to the container: `page.locator('main').getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue' }).click()`. The `main` element keeps the dialog's button out of the match.
